source.title: In-Context Learning of Linear Systems: Generalization Theory and Applications to Operator Learning
source.authors: Frank Cole; Yu-Long Lu; Wu-Zhe Xu; Tianhao Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and evaluates scaling of in-context generalization error with prompt lengths and number of training tasks. It does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute, or the compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper's scaling results concern generalization error for in-context linear systems and PDE operators as prompt lengths and task count vary. They do not measure the quantities in the listed claim versions. The paper also reports out-of-domain and task-diversity findings, but these do not test the listed scaling-law versions. Figure-based datapoints are not transcribed as numerical values.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and numerically checks error rates for a single-layer linear transformer solving linear systems/PDE operators in context, as functions of prompt lengths (n, m) and number of training tasks N. It calls these 'neural scaling laws' but measures in-context generalization error, not held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute, and has no model-size, compute-allocation, architecture-shape or downstream-from-loss analysis. Task count N and prompt length are sample sizes of a different construct, so no claim version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove in-domain error bounds in terms of task count and training/inference prompt lengths, show task diversity is necessary and sufficient for OOD generalization under task shifts (not covariate shifts), extend the bounds to in-context operator learning for linear elliptic PDEs, and report numerical rates consistent with the theory.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies a single-layer linear transformer for in-context linear systems and operator learning; it does not reproduce the language-model scaling-law method.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1 bounds in-domain in-context error by O(1/m + 1/n^2 + 1/sqrt(N)), improving to O(1/N) under a structural condition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For single-layer linear transformers learning linear systems in context, in-domain error decays as power laws in inference/training prompt length and number of pretraining tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-matrix experiments (d=10) show rates O(n^-2), O(m^-1), O(N^-1) matching the theory; PDE experiments (d=32) show O(n^-2), O(m^-1) and a faster unspecified rate in N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Empirical in-context error of linear transformers follows the theoretical power-law rates in prompt length and task count, in matrix and PDE operator settings.

record.problems: The numerical results are primarily presented in plots without stated individual datapoints or uncertainty estimates. The fast O(1/N) theoretical rate requires a structural condition that the authors say is difficult to verify; their experiments only suggest it holds. The studied rates concern in-context generalization error and sample sizes, not language-model pretraining loss or model scale.
record.rows_left_out: No plotted individual datapoints were extracted because exact values are not stated in the text. Other out-of-domain and task-diversity results were left out because they do not report a scaling result matching the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute in language models.
Extrapolation from small to large runs.
Depth/width effects at fixed parameter count (only single-layer models used).
Parameter/token/compute power laws in other modalities or regimes; the PDE setting scales prompt length and task count, not model or compute.
Downstream performance vs scale or pretraining loss.
Setup/fitting dependence of LM scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits.

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses the phrase 'neural scaling laws' for sample-size error bounds of a toy linear-attention model; this is a related but different construct from the LM pretraining scaling laws in the claim. Rates are read off log-log plots without stated values or uncertainty. Out-of-domain and diversity results (Figs. 2, 3, 5, 6) bear on no version and are rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of substantially larger language-model runs from power-law fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and how those quantities scale with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

The listed claim concerns the same parameter/token/compute scaling form in other modalities or training regimes; this paper measures prompt-length and task-count scaling of in-context generalization error instead.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from model scale or pretraining loss.
Whether the listed language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup and fitting choices.
